title: rp2 More USB woes
body:
I raise this in case it sheds any more light on the USB issues.
I am using `rp2-pico-20210209-unstable-v1.14-11-gc7aaee2b2.uf2`.

I have a substantial `uasyncio` application developed on Pyboards and ported to the Pico. The test script outputs regular messages via print statements. The application maintains a heartbeat LED via a coroutine on the Pico.

It runs fine if I suppress all print output.

With print statements enabled it also runs so long as I periodically press a key on the keyboard (in rshell or in miniterm). If I don't, it runs for a while then stops. The heartbeat stops flashing until I press a key, when running resumes. The code has evidently stalled.

Unfortunately my attempts to create a trivial test case have so far failed. I have never encountered this behaviour on Pyboards, ESP8266 or ESP32.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I should add that this application, while fairly involved, uses no "advanced" features of the chip. It communicates with an ESP8266 by bit banging, so doesn't use UART, I2C, SPI. It uses the Pin object but not interrupts. There is no use of native or viper emitters.

Here are the MicroPython modules imported by the various code modules:
```python
import uasyncio as asyncio
from utime import localtime, time
import sys  # sys.platform disables import of pyb and access to pyb.RTC
from micropython import const
import ujson
from machine import Pin  # The only "hardware" object
```

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I should also add what happens when I press a key as I think this must provide a clue.

The print statements comprise complete lines of text terminated with newlines. These are emitted at a low rate, a line every few seconds.

When the heartbeat stops flashing and I press Enter, the program resumes and many lines of text are emitted. Given the number of lines output it's clear that the program continued to run for several minutes before it stalled, with the text accumulating in a buffer. On receipt of a character the buffer emptied and the program resumed.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Is there are fixed time (always the same) for how long it takes before it pauses?  It may be that your PC is suspending the USB device so it goes to sleep, and only wakes when you type a key.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
We had a similar-sounding problem in CircuitPython recently. Copying multiple large files to the MSC drive would stall, then there would be a 30-second timeout, and USB would re-enumerate. The problem did not occur if there was a CDC REPL connection open to the board, even if there was no activity on that connection.

The problem was that `tud_task()` was not being scheduled to be called. [EDIT in bold] We used to **schedule a** call **to** `tud_task()` on every 1ms tick . Usually there was no work to do, but it got called promptly all the time. (It's cheap to call.) Then we started enqueuing an event to call it only after servicing a USB interrupt. If we were idle, we would do `WFI` to save power and just wait for an interrupt to trigger more work. This scheme worked most of the time, but we missed scheduling a `tud_task()` call in a particular circumstance. The [details](https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/pull/4122) are not really relevant to MicroPython because they have to do with our auto-reload mechanism. But they are related to scheduling `tud_task()`  properly when there is work to do, as is being discussed in #6835.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Thanks @participant2 , that's very interesting info (and relates to calling `tud_task()` from the USB IRQ handler).  Currently our rp2 port calls `tud_task()` all the time (eg every 1ms) so not sure that is the issue here.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> It may be that your PC is suspending the USB device so it goes to sleep, and only wakes when you type a key.

@participant1 I think this is unlikely as I have used this PC extensively with other MicroPython targets and never seen this before.

It also doesn't explain the symptoms (in my opinion).

While the program is running, no output is printed until I press Enter (or another key). Then, whatever output is pending is printed. Aside from the heartbeat, there is other evidence that the program is running normally while producing no printed output. If I don't press a key, it eventually stalls after nearly three minutes. Then pressing a key releases a torrent of (correct) output and the program resumes.

Another observation. The first time this happened I assumed my code had hung so I hit ctrl-c. To my surprise the Pico emitted many lines of output before producing a prompt. The code doesn't trap the keyboard interrupt. Presumably the code stopped immediately with the data being output by the underlying runtime.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I spoke too casually and perhaps misleadingly. In CircuitPython 5.x and before, we used to _schedule_ a call to `tud_task()` on every 1ms tick. We did not call it from the IRQ handler. We use `MICROPY_VM_HOOK_LOOP` to run background tasks, and running `tud_task()` (and many other background tasks) happened if 1ms had passed.

We subsequently revised the mechanism so that not every background task was called when 1ms had passed. Instead the tasks are enqueued when there is work to do. We no longer have a 1ms tick scheduling the overall set of background task. We still use `MICROPY_VM_HOOK_LOOP` (renamed to `RUN_BACKGROUND_TASKS`) and it does the queue checking, but only runs what is enqueued.

(Perhaps I should be repeating this in #6835.)

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
OK, here is a trivial test case. Paste at the REPL. I left this running for many minutes before going back to examine progress,
```python
import time
while True:
    print('got here')
    time.sleep(30)
```
It printed output once only, only emitting queued output when I press a key. The slow rate seems to be crucial, my other attempts at test cases emitted output at high speed. These ran without error.

[EDIT]
Just to nail the possibility of a PC issue I ran the same script on a Pyboard. It did not exhibit this behaviour, working as expected even when I left it unattended for some time.

On the rp2 it behaves like my application. If I press a key, any pending output is emitted. Until I do it is silent.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
This test case (run on the rp2) behaves in exactly the same way as my application. I added the obligatory LED flasher:
```python
import time
from machine import Pin
led = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)
while True:
    print('got here')
    led(not led())
    time.sleep(30)
```
which shows that the script continues to run while producing no output, but it eventually stalls. Pressing a key causes it to emit output and to resume running.

comments.body:
The script produces only one line. If I hit a key, it produces as many lines as are buffered at that time. I didn't time how long it took to actually stall, I'd guess at about 15 minutes (30 iterations).

I've tried reducing the delay. At 2 seconds or below it works perfectly. At 3 seconds it behaves as described, emitting only one line until I press a key.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
OK, this prompted me to try other PC's. On my three other machines the fault does not appear even with 30s timing. The two desktops are elderly so USB2. The other laptop is USB3. One of the desktops uses a hub. All run fairly recent Ubuntu or Mint.

So it's just this laptop.

There must be something odd about the USB implementation on this laptop. It's a two year old Dell Precision 5530 Core i5-8300H - a fairly high-end machine. It runs Ubuntu 20.04. I use it heavily for MicroPython on Pyboards, ESP8266 and ESP32 and have had no issues with USB. I have changed nothing in its setup and the same script ran with this machine on a Pyboard 1.1.

I therefore do believe there is an issue with the rp2 USB, but I've clearly struck unlucky with my usual PC.

I didn't realise it was Linux specific... @participant4 can replicate on his Linux machine so we can investigate from there.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
This problem keeps cropping up in the forum, with people thinking their script has failed when in fact it is the USB communication which has stopped. 

The defining characteristic is that increasing the message rate makes the fault go away. [This](https://forum.micropython.org/viewtopic.php?f=21&t=9988) is the most recent instance.
